description:
EXPLORATION OF THE SALTICIDAE FAMILY
	The collected species that I’ve chosen to do is a spider that is called Phidippus audax. Also known as a Daring or Bold Jumping spider. The taxonomy of this species are that the kingdom is an Animalia and the Phylum is Arthropoda. The subphylum is called Chelicerata and there are different kinds of jumping spiders. The class that spiders are in and including this one is called Arachnida, the order is Araneae. The suborder of this species is Opisthothelae and the infraorder is Araneomorphae. The Family that Jumping spiders are identified as is called Salticidae.
	The Morphological traits of the Jumping spider are that it is black with white hair, and with blue greenish Chelicera’s. It has four pairs of eyes which is very different to most spiders that have eight eyes, they have one pair that is their particularly large anterior median eyes. They have little strips of white going down their abdomen and a have an oddly shape of a cephalothorax, with a rectangular type of face that are perpendicular to their direction of motion. Their fangs are largely medium size and the pedipalps are also. The legs of the jumping spider aren’t covered with any very prominent spines, their front four generally are bigger than the hind four. 	
	The Phidippus audax and Phidippus johnsoni are very closely alike since there are both jumping spiders. They are in the same Genus (Phidippus) and the same Family (Salticidae). These both species have colorful Chelicera’s of blue greenish colors, all of the jumping spiders have four pairs of eyes with one pair that is their large anterior median eyes. Both species have legs that have four of them bigger than the hind four. They both have the same shape of their cephalothorax, with a rectangular face as the same motion of the vision. 
	The reproductive processes of Jumping spiders are kind of complex, but visual courtship displays using both movements and physical bodily attributes. Unlike females, males possess plumose hairs, colored or iridescent hairs, front leg fringes, structures on other legs, often bizarre, modifications. These characteristics are used in a courtship "dance" in which the colored or iridescent parts of the body are displayed. In addition to the display of hairs jumping spiders perform complex sideling, vibrational, or zigzag movements to attract females. If receptive to the male, the female will assume a passive, crouching position. It has also recently been discovered that many males have auditory signals as well. These amplified sounds produced by the males, resemble buzzes or drum rolls, which are presented to the female. In some species, the female may also vibrate her palps or abdomen. The male will then extend his front legs towards the female to touch her. If the female remains receptive, the male will climb on the female's back and inseminate her with his palps. Daring jumping spiders reach maturation in the springtime, and mating begins around late spring or early summer. Reproductive females will produce as many as eight eggs sacs per year with each egg sac containing from 30-170 eggs. The spiders living in the warmer portions of their distribution range usually live longer and produce more offspring.
	I collected my species at my house where I have little bit of big trees and small ones. I found my Daring jumping spider just below my tree in the dirt crawling around. Although I did find another one in the gravel, they usually can live in a variety of habitats like Tropical forests. They can also live in temperate forests, scrub lands, deserts, intertidal zones, and mountainous regions. 
	The adaptations of P. audax are the eight eyes. The forward-facing anterior median eyes are the largest of all the eyes. When a person looks at the spider, the eyes are the ones that look back at that person. To the side of the eyes are the smaller anterior lateral eyes. Behind the eyes, and almost on top of the head, are the posterior median (PM) eyes and posterior lateral (PL) eyes. Jumping spiders have very keen eyesight. Eyesight is essential for hunting and courting. Now comparing to my other selected species the rest have eight that are all in front of the face.

description:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phidippus_audax

Phidippus audax is a common jumping spider of North America. It is commonly referred to as the daring jumping spider, or bold jumping spider. The average size of adults ranges from roughly 13–20 millimetres (0.51–0.79 in) in length. They are typically black with a pattern of spots and stripes on their abdomen and legs. Often these spots are orange-tinted in juveniles, turning white as the spider matures. The spider belongs to the genus Phidippus, a group of jumping spiders easily identified both by their relatively large size and their iridescent chelicerae. In the case of P. audax, these chelicerae are a bright, metallic green or blue.
These spiders have been known to jump from 10 to 50 times their own body length by suddenly increasing the blood pressure in the third or fourth pair of legs,[1][2] and the male may jump away during mating if the female approaches too quickly.[3]

description:
Drinking water from a q-tip.  Found the previous night in the basement. She seemed weak, just sat in my hand not moving much. I tried offering drops of water on my hand but she was not interested.  I put her in a container with a silverfish I caught but she didn't attempt to eat it.  

Today she looked even worse, sitting with legs curled under.  I then offered water on a q-tip (thanks internet!) and she took it right away!  She drank twice, pausing for several minutes in between.  

After drinking she rested for a hour or so and then she chased and caught the silverfish!  She looked much more lively and curious like a normal jumping spider.  

Checked on her a couple hours later and the shriveled up silverfish was cast aside.  She was crawling around underneath a little cardboard hut I placed in the container.  

There's no lid on the container, so we'll see how long she sticks around.  Glad I was able to give some assistance.  Jumping spiders are the best.

description:
Honda the bold jumper! I named him that because he somehow lived behind the glovebox of my Accord for a few days without food and through sweltering heat. I first found him on my passenger window while parked, so I rolled the window down to say hi. I guess that spooked him and he scurried into the car, stopping briefly on the door handle to make eye contact before booking it to the space under the glovebox. I tried to catch him but he was too fast, lol. I bet I looked really strange in the parking lot bending over my dash/cup holders to root around in the space where the passenger’s feet go. 
I left it at that and said RIP since my car has a black interior and it was really hot that day…
A couple days later I was driving home from graduation commencement rehearsal and he was just sitting on my dash! I saw him and said out loud “Oh hi, I thought you died!”
I glanced at him every few seconds as I exited the highway to keep track of him; he crawled from the dash to the ashtray(where I keep my receipts lol) to the little space with the USB outlets, where he hung out until I got home. I managed to prod him into my coin cup(which had been emptied beforehand) and paparazzi him before depositing him onto a gas pipeline pole where he could get some sun and find food. 
If you read this whole thing, fave this observation, and I’m
sorry for making you read it lol
Beautiful jumping spider, huge for what I’ve normally seen, the pine needle gives a great reference about the size. In love with this little girl.
